extra.message: The `username` value taken directly from the JSON request body (sqli.py:10) is interpolated into a SQL string with an f-string and passed to `cur.execute()`. No parameterised query or escaping is used, so an attacker can terminate the quoted literal (e.g. `' OR '1'='1`) and execute arbitrary SQL against the SQLite database, dumping the USERS table or other data.

cwe: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

extra.message: The attacker-controlled `mathexp` field from the request body is concatenated into a Jinja2 `Template` source string and then rendered with `test.render()` (ssti.py:12). Because the untrusted data becomes part of the template itself rather than a rendering context variable, an attacker can inject Jinja2 expressions (e.g. `{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}` or config/global traversal) to read server state and achieve remote code execution.

cwe: CWE-1336: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine
CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

extra.message: `fetchfile()` passes its `name` argument straight to `open()` with no canonicalisation, base-directory confinement, or allowlist. It is reached from the `/api/lfivuln` handler with the user-supplied `filename` body field (lfi.py:13,16), so a request containing `../../../../etc/passwd` or an absolute path reads arbitrary files from the server filesystem and returns their contents in the JSON response.

cwe: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

extra.message: The `/api/lfivuln` endpoint lets the client fully control which file the server opens: `filename` is read from the JSON body (lfi.py:13) and used verbatim to select the file read target via `fetchfile()`. There is no validation that the resolved path stays inside an intended directory and no allowlist of permitted filenames, so the external input controls the file system resource being accessed.

cwe: CWE-73: External Control of File Name or Path

extra.message: `fetchimage()` issues `requests.get(url=name, ...)` where `name` originates from the client-supplied `imagelink` body field of `/api/rfivuln` (rfi.py:15,18). No scheme allowlist, host allowlist, or private-address filtering is applied, and the full response body is returned to the caller. An attacker can force the server to request internal endpoints (e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, `http://127.0.0.1:8000/`) or `file://`-style targets and read the response, a classic server-side request forgery / remote file inclusion.

The application is started with `debug=True` while also binding to all interfaces (`host="0.0.0.0"`). This enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger and auto-reloader in whatever environment the app is launched in; anyone who can reach the port and trigger an unhandled exception gets an interactive Python console (guessable/derivable PIN) and therefore remote code execution, plus full stack traces and source code disclosure. Debug functionality must never be active on a network-reachable deployment.

cwe: CWE-215: Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Debugging Code

extra.message: The `/api/sqlivuln` login handler reads both `username` and `password` but the authentication query only filters on `USERNAME` — `password` is never compared against the stored value, and any non-empty password succeeds. The handler then returns the matching user rows (including the stored password) as the response. Authentication is therefore effectively bypassed for any known username, e.g. `admin` with an arbitrary password.

The raw database exception text is returned to the client in the HTTP 200 response body. SQLite error messages leak schema details (table and column names, syntax context) and greatly ease exploitation of the SQL injection on line 16 by turning it into an error-based oracle.

cwe: CWE-209: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

extra.message: The `/api/hhivuln` password-reset handler takes the client-controlled `Host` request header (hhi.py:12) and embeds it unescaped into the `href` attribute of an anchor tag returned to the user. An attacker who controls the Host header can point the reset link at an arbitrary domain (password-reset poisoning, cache poisoning) and, because the value is interpolated into HTML with no attribute escaping, can also break out of the quoted attribute to inject arbitrary markup/script.

cwe: CWE-644: Improper Neutralization of HTTP Headers for Scripting Syntax
CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

extra.message: The `/api/xssreflected` handler reflects the client-supplied `username` body field back into the response body with no output encoding or sanitisation. Any consumer that renders this `msg` value as HTML (including the bundled Swagger UI and any front-end that interpolates the field) will execute injected script, e.g. `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`.

cwe: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

extra.message: The OpenAPI specification that defines every route (`app.add_api("swagger.yml")` in app.py:17) declares no `securitySchemes` and no global or per-operation `security` requirement, and none of the handler modules perform any identity or permission check. Security-sensitive operations — arbitrary file read (`/lfivuln`), outbound request forgery (`/rfivuln`), template rendering (`/sstivuln`) and the login/user-lookup endpoint (`/sqlivuln`) — are therefore reachable by any unauthenticated remote client.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: The `/api/sqlivuln` credential-checking endpoint has no rate limiting, throttling, CAPTCHA, or account-lockout logic. There is no limiter middleware anywhere in the request path — `app.py` registers only `connexion.App` with the raw swagger spec and no before-request hook or WSGI middleware — so an attacker can submit unlimited credential guesses (and unlimited SQL-injection probes) against this endpoint at full speed.

cwe: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

extra.message: The login/credential-lookup path produces no security audit record: successful lookups, failed lookups (empty result set), and database errors are all returned to the client without any logging call. No shared logging middleware, before/after-request hook, or handler-level logger exists anywhere in the application (only ad-hoc `print()` of raw headers in hhi.py), so authentication attempts and failures leave no durable trail for detection or forensics.

Database seeding hardcodes two application accounts and their credentials in source — `mike`/`kaines` and `admin`/`admin`. The passwords are stored as cleartext in the USERS table (no hashing or salting), and combined with the login handler in sqli.py these give a remote attacker a known-good administrative username.

cwe: CWE-256: Plaintext Storage of a Password

extra.message: `requests.get(..., verify=False)` disables TLS certificate and hostname verification for the outbound fetch, so any HTTPS URL retrieved by this endpoint can be transparently intercepted or modified by a network attacker, and the fetched content is returned to the API caller as trusted output.
